go_v2_6.3.31.q:
In the context-free grammar below, $S$ is the start symbol, $a$ and $b$ are terminals, and $\epsilon$ denotes the empty string.

$S \to aSa \mid bSb \mid a \mid b \mid \epsilon$

Which of the following strings is NOT generated by the grammar?
go_v2_6.3.31.e:
**Key idea:** $S \to aSa \mid bSb$ always wraps the same symbol on both ends. The base cases $\epsilon$, $a$, $b$ give an even-length or odd-length centre. So the grammar generates exactly the **palindromes** over $\{a,b\}$.

| String | Palindrome? | Derivation |
|---|---|---|
| $aaaa$ | yes | $S \Rightarrow aSa \Rightarrow aaSaa \Rightarrow aaaa$ |
| $baba$ | **no** (first symbol $b$, last symbol $a$) | none |
| $abba$ | yes | $S \Rightarrow aSa \Rightarrow abSba \Rightarrow abba$ |
| $babaaabab$ | yes (centre $a$) | $S \Rightarrow bSb \Rightarrow baSab \Rightarrow babSbab \Rightarrow babaSabab \Rightarrow babaaabab$ |

Every nonempty generated string begins and ends with the same symbol, so $baba$ cannot be generated.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v2_6.3.32.q:
The two grammars given below generate a language over the alphabet $\{x, y, z\}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
G1:\ & S \rightarrow x \mid z \mid xS \mid zS \mid yB \\
     & B \rightarrow y \mid z \mid yB \mid zB \\[4pt]
G2:\ & S \rightarrow y \mid z \mid yS \mid zS \mid xB \\
     & B \rightarrow y \mid yS
\end{aligned}
$$

Which one of the following choices describes the properties satisfied by the strings in these languages?
o: $G1$: No $y$ appears before any $x$; $G2$: Every $x$ is followed by at least one $y$
$G1$: No $y$ appears before any $x$; $G2$: No $x$ appears before any $y$
$G1$: No $y$ appears after any $x$; $G2$: Every $x$ is followed by at least one $y$
$G1$: No $y$ appears after any $x$; $G2$: Every $y$ is followed by at least one $x$
go_v2_6.3.32.e:
**Key idea:** Both grammars are right-linear, so read them like automata. $S$ and $B$ act as states, and each production emits one terminal.

**$G1$.** From $S$ we can emit $x$ or $z$ and stay in $S$. Once a $y$ is emitted we move to $B$, and $B$ only ever emits $y$ or $z$. Hence
$$L(G1) = (x+z)^*(x+z)\ \cup\ (x+z)^*\,y\,(y+z)^+ .$$
After the first $y$ no $x$ can appear, so **no $y$ appears before any $x$**. The statement in (C)/(D), "no $y$ appears after any $x$", is false: $S \Rightarrow xS \Rightarrow xyB \Rightarrow xyy$ has a $y$ after an $x$.

**$G2$.** From $S$ we may emit $y$ or $z$ freely. Emitting $x$ moves to $B$, whose only productions are $B \to y \mid yS$, so every $x$ is immediately followed by a $y$:
$$L(G2) = (y + z + xy)^+ .$$
So **every $x$ is followed by at least one $y$**.
- (B)'s "no $x$ appears before any $y$" fails for $xy$ ($S \Rightarrow xB \Rightarrow xy$).
- (D)'s "every $y$ is followed by at least one $x$" fails for the one-symbol string $y$ ($S \Rightarrow y$).

Only option (A) is right for both grammars.

**Answer: (A)**

go_v2_6.3.34.q:
Consider the following grammars. Names representing terminals have been specified in capital letters.

$$
\begin{array}{|llll|}
\hline
G_1: & \text{stmnt} & \rightarrow & \text{WHILE (expr) stmnt} \\
 & \text{stmnt} & \rightarrow & \text{OTHER} \\
 & \text{expr} & \rightarrow & \text{ID} \\
\hline
G_2: & \text{stmnt} & \rightarrow & \text{WHILE (expr) stmnt} \\
 & \text{stmnt} & \rightarrow & \text{OTHER} \\
 & \text{expr} & \rightarrow & \text{expr + expr} \\
 & \text{expr} & \rightarrow & \text{expr * expr} \\
 & \text{expr} & \rightarrow & \text{ID} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$

Which one of the following statements is true?
o: $G_1$ is context-free but not regular and $G_2$ is regular
$G_2$ is context-free but not regular and $G_1$ is regular
Both $G_1$ and $G_2$ are context-free but neither of them is regular
go_v2_6.3.34.e:
**Key idea:** The options classify the *grammars*. A grammar is regular (type 3) only if all its productions are right-linear ($A \to wB$ or $A \to w$, with $w$ a string of terminals), or all are left-linear.

- In both grammars, $\text{stmnt} \to \text{WHILE (expr) stmnt}$ has **two** nonterminals ($\text{expr}$ and $\text{stmnt}$) on the right-hand side, so it is neither right- nor left-linear.
- $G_2$ also has $\text{expr} \to \text{expr + expr}$ and $\text{expr} \to \text{expr * expr}$, again with two nonterminals.
- Every production has a single nonterminal on the left, so both grammars are context-free.

Hence both are context-free grammars and neither is a regular grammar, which gives **(D)**.

**Caution: the languages themselves are regular.** $\text{expr}$ never produces a parenthesis, and $\text{stmnt}$ recurses only at its right end, so there is no unbounded nesting:
$$L(G_1) = \big(\texttt{WHILE}\ \texttt{(}\ \texttt{ID}\ \texttt{)}\big)^*\ \texttt{OTHER}$$
$$L(G_2) = \Big(\texttt{WHILE}\ \texttt{(}\ \texttt{ID}\,\big((\texttt{+} \mid \texttt{*})\,\texttt{ID}\big)^*\ \texttt{)}\Big)^*\ \texttt{OTHER}$$
Equivalent right-linear grammars therefore exist. If "regular" in the options meant "generates a regular language", then (C) would be the true statement. Read literally as a statement about the given grammars, (D) is correct. (A) and (B) are wrong under either reading, because they treat the two grammars differently.

**Answer: (D)**
go_v2_6.3.34.note: Read literally, the options classify the grammars as written: both are context-free grammars and neither is a regular (right- or left-linear) grammar, so (D) is the accepted answer. The languages they generate are in fact regular, so if "regular" were read as a property of the languages, (C) would be the true statement.

go_v2_6.3.35.q:
Consider a CFG with the following productions.

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &\rightarrow AA \mid B \\
A &\rightarrow 0A \mid A0 \mid 1 \\
B &\rightarrow 0B00 \mid 1
\end{aligned}
$$

$S$ is the start symbol, $A$ and $B$ are non-terminals and 0 and 1 are the terminals. The language generated by this grammar is:
o: The set of all strings over $\{0, 1\}$ containing at least two 0's
go_v2_6.3.35.e:
**Key idea:** Work out what each nonterminal generates, then combine.

- $A \to 0A \mid A0 \mid 1$: starting from the single $1$, we can add $0$'s on the left ($0A$) and on the right ($A0$) any number of times. So $L(A) = \{0^i 1 0^j \mid i, j \ge 0\}$.
- $B \to 0B00 \mid 1$: each use of $0B00$ adds one $0$ on the left and two on the right. So $L(B) = \{0^n 1 0^{2n} \mid n \ge 0\}$, e.g. $1,\ 0100,\ 0010000$.
- $S \to AA$: joining two $A$-strings gives $0^i 1 0^{j} 0^{j'} 1 0^k = 0^i 1 0^{j+j'} 1 0^k$. Since $j+j'$ can be any value $\ge 0$, $L(AA) = \{0^i 1 0^j 1 0^k \mid i, j, k \ge 0\}$.

Therefore
$$L(G) = \{0^i 1 0^j 1 0^k \mid i,j,k \ge 0\} \cup \{0^n 1 0^{2n} \mid n \ge 0\},$$
which is option (B).

**Why the others fail:**
- (A) misses $11$ (from $AA$) and $1$ (from $B$ with $n=0$).
- (C) contains $01$. A string with a single $1$ can come only from $B$, which needs twice as many $0$'s after the $1$ as before it, so $01 \notin L(G)$.
- (D) contains $000$, which has no $1$, yet every generated string has one or two $1$'s. Also $11 \in L(G)$ has no $0$ at all.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v2_6.5.3.q: State the halting problem of the Turing machine.
go_v2_6.5.3.e:
**Statement.** The halting problem asks the following. Given (an encoding of) an arbitrary Turing machine $M$ and an arbitrary input string $w$, does $M$ halt on $w$?

As a language:
$$\mathrm{HALT}_{TM} = \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ is a TM and } M \text{ halts on input } w\}.$$
The question is whether some single algorithm (a TM that halts on every input) can answer this correctly for every pair $\langle M, w\rangle$.

**Status: undecidable** (Turing, 1936). No such algorithm exists.
- The problem is *partially decidable*, i.e. recursively enumerable. A universal TM simulates $M$ on $w$ and answers "yes" if the simulation halts.
- That simulator never answers "no" when $M$ runs forever.
- The complement, "does $M$ loop forever on $w$?", is not even recursively enumerable.

**Proof sketch (diagonalization).**
1. Suppose some TM $H$ decides $\mathrm{HALT}_{TM}$.
2. Build a TM $D$. On input $\langle M\rangle$, $D$ runs $H$ on $\langle M, \langle M\rangle\rangle$. If $H$ says "halts", $D$ loops forever; if $H$ says "loops", $D$ halts.
3. Run $D$ on $\langle D\rangle$:
   - if $D$ halts on $\langle D\rangle$, then $H$ said "loops", a contradiction;
   - if $D$ loops on $\langle D\rangle$, then $H$ said "halts", again a contradiction.

So $H$ cannot exist.

**Answer: Given an arbitrary TM $M$ and input $w$, decide whether $M$ halts on $w$. This problem is undecidable (only semi-decidable).**

go_v2_6.5.9.q:
Suppose we have a function HALTS which when applied to any arbitrary function $f$ and its arguments will say TRUE if function $f$ terminates for those arguments and FALSE otherwise. Example: Given the following function definition.

```
FACTORIAL (N) = IF (N=0) THEN 1 ELSE N*FACTORIAL (N-1)
```

Then HALTS (FACTORIAL, 4) = TRUE and HALTS (FACTORIAL, -5) = FALSE

Let us define the function `FUNNY (f) = IF HALTS (f) THEN not (f) ELSE TRUE`

(a) Show that FUNNY terminates for all functions $f$.

(b) use (a) to prove (by contradiction) that it is not possible to have a function like HALTS which for arbitrary functions and inputs says whether it will terminate on that input or not.
go_v2_6.5.9.e:
**How to read the definition.**
- `HALTS(f)` means `HALTS(f, f)`: does $f$ terminate when it is given itself as its argument?
- `not(f)` means `not(f(f))`.

So
$$\text{FUNNY}(f) = \begin{cases} \neg\, f(f) & \text{if } f(f) \text{ terminates},\\ \text{TRUE} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

**(a) FUNNY terminates for every $f$.** Assume HALTS exists. By hypothesis it always returns TRUE or FALSE in finite time. There are two cases.
- If HALTS$(f, f)$ = FALSE, FUNNY returns TRUE at once.
- If HALTS$(f, f)$ = TRUE, then $f(f)$ terminates with some value $v$. FUNNY computes $f(f)$, which takes finitely many steps, and returns $\neg v$.

In both cases FUNNY$(f)$ terminates, so FUNNY is a total function.

**(b) HALTS cannot exist.** FUNNY is itself a function, so we may apply it to itself.
1. By (a), FUNNY(FUNNY) terminates. Hence HALTS(FUNNY, FUNNY) = TRUE.
2. So the THEN branch of FUNNY's definition is taken:
$$\text{FUNNY(FUNNY)} = \neg\, \text{FUNNY(FUNNY)}.$$
3. Let $v$ be the value of FUNNY(FUNNY), which exists by (a). Then $v = \neg v$, and no truth value satisfies this.

Seen operationally, evaluating FUNNY(FUNNY) would call FUNNY(FUNNY) again and recurse forever, which contradicts (a).

The only assumption used was that a total, always-correct HALTS exists, so that assumption is false. No algorithm can decide, for arbitrary functions and inputs, whether the function terminates. This is the undecidability of the halting problem, proved by diagonalization.

**Answer: (a) FUNNY is total, because HALTS always returns and $f(f)$ is evaluated only when it halts. (b) Then FUNNY(FUNNY) $= \neg$FUNNY(FUNNY), a contradiction, so HALTS cannot exist.**

go_v2_6.5.12.q:
Let a decision problem $X$ be defined as follows:

$X$: Given a Turing machine $M$ over $\Sigma$ and any word $w \in \Sigma$, does $M$ loop forever on $w$?

You may assume that the halting problem of Turing machine is undecidable but partially decidable.

(a) Show that $X$ is undecidable

(b) Show that $X$ is not even partially decidable
go_v2_6.5.12.e:
**Key observation.** For every instance $\langle M, w\rangle$, "$M$ loops forever on $w$" means exactly "$M$ does not halt on $w$". So
$$X = \overline{\mathrm{HALT}},$$
the complement of the halting problem. Checking whether an input is a well-formed encoding is decidable, so ill-formed inputs do not affect the argument.

**(a) $X$ is undecidable.**
1. Suppose a TM $D_X$ decides $X$, i.e. it halts on every input with the correct yes/no answer.
2. Build $D_H$: on input $\langle M, w\rangle$, run $D_X$ and output the opposite answer.
3. $D_H$ always halts. It says "yes" exactly when $M$ does not loop forever on $w$, that is, when $M$ halts on $w$.
4. So $D_H$ decides HALT, contradicting the undecidability of HALT.

Hence $X$ is undecidable. In short, decidable problems are closed under complement.

**(b) $X$ is not even partially decidable.**
1. Suppose $X$ were partially decidable, with a TM $P_X$ that halts with "yes" exactly on the instances of $X$.
2. HALT is partially decidable by assumption, through a TM $P_H$ that simulates $M$ on $w$ and says "yes" if the simulation halts.
3. Decide HALT as follows. On $\langle M, w\rangle$, run $P_H$ and $P_X$ alternately, one step each (dovetailing).
   - Every instance belongs to exactly one of HALT and $X$, so exactly one of the two machines eventually says "yes", after finitely many steps.
   - If $P_H$ says "yes", answer "halts". If $P_X$ says "yes", answer "loops".
4. This procedure always halts and is always correct, so HALT would be decidable, a contradiction.

Hence $X$ is not partially decidable (not recursively enumerable). The general fact used here: if a language and its complement are both RE, the language is recursive.

**Answer: $X = \overline{\text{HALT}}$, so (a) it is undecidable, and (b) it is not even partially decidable, since otherwise HALT would be decidable.**

go_v2_6.5.13.q:
The aim of the following question is to prove that the language $\{M \mid M \text{ is the code of the Turing Machine which, irrespective of the input, halts and outputs a } 1\}$, is undecidable. This is to be done by reducing from the language $\{M', x \mid M' \text{ halts on } x\}$, which is known to be undecidable. In parts (a) and (b) describe the $2$ main steps in the construction of $M$. In part (c) describe the key property which relates the behaviour of $M$ on its input $w$ to the behaviour of $M'$ on $x$.

(a) On input $w$, what is the first step that $M$ must make?

(b) On input $w$, based on the outcome of the first step, what is the second step $M$ must make?

(c) What key property relates the behaviour of $M$ on $w$ to the behaviour of $M'$ on $x$?
go_v2_6.5.13.e:
**Setting up the reduction.** Let
$$L = \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ halts and outputs } 1 \text{ on every input}\}.$$
From an instance $\langle M', x\rangle$ of the halting problem, we build, by an algorithm, a machine $M = M_{M',x}$ with $M'$ and $x$ hard-coded into it.

**(a) First step.** On input $w$, $M$ erases $w$ (it ignores its own input), writes $x$ on the tape, and simulates $M'$ on $x$.

**(b) Second step.**
- If the simulation of $M'$ on $x$ halts, $M$ erases the tape, writes $1$ and halts.
- If $M'$ never halts on $x$, the simulation runs forever. $M$ then never reaches this step and never halts.

**(c) Key property.** The behaviour of $M$ does not depend on $w$:
$$\forall w:\quad M \text{ halts on } w \text{ with output } 1 \iff M' \text{ halts on } x.$$
- If $M'$ halts on $x$, then $M$ halts and outputs 1 on every input.
- Otherwise $M$ halts on no input at all.

Therefore $\langle M\rangle \in L \iff \langle M', x\rangle \in \mathrm{HALT}$.

**Conclusion.** The map $\langle M', x\rangle \mapsto \langle M\rangle$ is computable, since it only writes out the code of $M$. Suppose $L$ had a decider $D$. Running $D$ on $\langle M\rangle$ would then decide whether $M'$ halts on $x$, which is impossible. Hence $L$ is undecidable.

**Answer: (a) Ignore $w$ and simulate $M'$ on $x$. (b) If the simulation halts, output 1 and halt. (c) $M$ halts with output 1 on every $w$ (equivalently, on any $w$) iff $M'$ halts on $x$.**

go_v2_6.5.14.q:
Consider two languages $L_1$ and $L_2$ each on the alphabet $\Sigma$. Let $f: \Sigma^* \rightarrow \Sigma^*$ be a polynomial time computable bijection such that $(\forall x)[x \in L_1 \text{ iff } f(x) \in L_2]$. Further, let $f^{-1}$ be also polynomial time computable.

Which of the following **CANNOT** be true?
o: $L_1$ is recursively enumerable and $L_2$ is recursive
go_v2_6.5.14.e:
**Key idea:** $f$ is a computable many-one reduction from $L_1$ to $L_2$. Because $f$ is a bijection, $y \in L_2 \iff f^{-1}(y) \in L_1$, so $f^{-1}$ is a reduction from $L_2$ to $L_1$. The two languages are therefore equally hard, and every "easier than" argument works in both directions.

**(C) cannot be true.** Suppose $L_2$ is decidable. To decide $L_1$ on input $x$, compute $f(x)$ (which halts) and run the decider for $L_2$ on it. This answers "$x \in L_1$?" correctly, so $L_1$ is decidable too. Hence $L_1$ cannot be undecidable while $L_2$ is decidable.

The other three options are all possible:
- **(A)** If $L_2$ is finite, then $L_1 = f^{-1}(L_2)$ is finite and therefore in P. For example, take $L_1 = L_2 = \varnothing$ with $f$ the identity.
- **(B)** If $L_2 \in P$, then $L_1 \in P \subseteq NP$, because $f$ runs in polynomial time. This is consistent.
- **(D)** If $L_2$ is recursive, then $L_1$ is recursive and hence also recursively enumerable. This is consistent.

**Answer: (C)**

go_v2_6.5.16.q: Which of the following problems is undecidable?
go_v2_6.5.16.e:
**(A) Decidable.** To test whether $w \in L(G)$ for a CFG $G$, convert $G$ to Chomsky normal form and run the CYK algorithm, which takes $O(|w|^3)$ time.

**(B) Undecidable.** No algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary CFG is ambiguous. The standard proof reduces Post's Correspondence Problem to it: a PCP instance has a solution iff a grammar built from it is ambiguous.

**(C) Decidable.** Remove useless states from the FSA. $L(A)$ is infinite iff there is a cycle on some path from the start state to a final state. Equivalently, it is infinite iff $A$ accepts some string whose length is between $n$ and $2n-1$, where $n$ is the number of states.

**(D) Decidable.** $L(A_1) = L(A_2)$ iff the symmetric difference $(L_1 \cap \overline{L_2}) \cup (\overline{L_1} \cap L_2)$ is empty. This can be checked with product automata and an emptiness test. Alternatively, minimise both DFAs and check whether they are isomorphic.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v2_6.5.24.q: Let $A$ and $B$ be finite alphabets and let $\#$ be a symbol outside both $A$ and $B$. Let $f$ be a total function from $A^*$ to $B^*$. We say $f$ is *computable* if there exists a Turing machine $M$ which given an input $x \in A^*$, always halts with $f(x)$ on its tape. Let $L_f$ denote the language $\{x \# f(x) \mid x \in A^*\}$. Which of the following statements is true:
o: $f$ is computable if and only if $L_f$ is recursive.
$f$ is computable if and only if $L_f$ is recursively enumerable.
If $f$ is computable then $L_f$ is recursive, but not conversely.
If $f$ is computable then $L_f$ is recursively enumerable, but not conversely.
go_v2_6.5.24.e:
**Key idea.** $L_f$ is just the graph of $f$, written as strings. Since $\#$ is in neither $A$ nor $B$, a string $x\#z$ with $x \in A^*$ and $z \in B^*$ splits in only one way, and $x\#z \in L_f$ exactly when $z = f(x)$. Because $f$ is **total**, every $x$ has exactly one such $z$, so computing $f(x)$ comes down to finding the one $z$ with $x\#z \in L_f$.

**Step 1: $f$ computable $\Rightarrow$ $L_f$ recursive.** Let $M$ compute $f$. On input $u$:
1. If $u$ is not of the form $x\#z$ with $x \in A^*$ and $z \in B^*$, reject.
2. Otherwise run $M$ on $x$. It halts with $f(x)$. Accept iff $z = f(x)$.

This procedure always halts, so $L_f$ is recursive, and therefore also recursively enumerable.

**Step 2: $L_f$ recursively enumerable $\Rightarrow$ $f$ computable.** Let $R$ be a Turing machine that accepts exactly $L_f$; it may loop forever on strings outside $L_f$. Let $z_1, z_2, \dots$ be all strings of $B^*$ in length-lexicographic order. On input $x$, for $k = 1, 2, 3, \dots$:
- run $R$ for $k$ steps on each of $x\#z_1, \dots, x\#z_k$;
- if one of them, say $x\#z_i$, is accepted, output $z_i$ and halt.

Suppose $f(x) = z_j$ and $R$ accepts $x\#z_j$ in $s$ steps. Then the search succeeds by round $\max(j, s)$ at the latest. No string $x\#z$ with $z \ne f(x)$ belongs to $L_f$, so nothing else is ever accepted and the output is exactly $f(x)$. The procedure always halts, so $f$ is computable.

The interleaving (dovetailing) matters here. Running $R$ to completion on $x\#z_1$, then on $x\#z_2$, and so on could hang forever on some $z_i \ne f(x)$. A recursive language is also recursively enumerable, so Step 2 also proves "$L_f$ recursive $\Rightarrow$ $f$ computable". With a decider, you can simply test $z_1, z_2, \dots$ one at a time.

**Conclusion.** For a total function $f$,
$$f \text{ computable} \iff L_f \text{ recursive} \iff L_f \text{ recursively enumerable}.$$

- **(A)** True. Step 1 gives one direction and Step 2 the other.
- **(C)** False. "Not conversely" claims that $L_f$ recursive does not imply $f$ computable, but it does (Step 2).
- **(D)** False. "Not conversely" claims that $L_f$ recursively enumerable does not imply $f$ computable, but Step 2 shows it does.
- **(B)** Also a true statement. Steps 1 and 2 give both of its directions, so strictly speaking (A) and (B) are both correct. The intended answer is (A), the standard fact that a total function is computable iff its graph is decidable.

**Answer: (A)**
go_v2_6.5.24.note: Because f is total, even a merely recursively enumerable L_f makes f computable (dovetail a recognizer over all candidate outputs), so statement (B) is also true and strictly two options are correct; the official answer is (A).

go_v2_6.5.25.q:
Let $L(R)$ be the language represented by regular expression $R$. Let $L(G)$ be the language generated by a context free grammar $G$. Let $L(M)$ be the language accepted by a Turing machine $M$. Which of the following decision problems are undecidable?

I. Given a regular expression $R$ and a string $w$, is $w \in L(R)$?

II. Given a context-free grammar $G$, is $L(G) = \emptyset$

III. Given a context-free grammar $G$, is $L(G) = \Sigma^*$ for some alphabet $\Sigma$?

IV. Given a Turing machine $M$ and a string $w$, is $w \in L(M)$?
go_v2_6.5.25.e:
**I is decidable.** Convert $R$ to an NFA (Thompson's construction) and simulate it on $w$, or convert it to a DFA and run that.

**II is decidable.** Mark the *generating* variables iteratively. A variable is generating if one of its productions has a body made only of terminals and already-marked variables. $L(G) = \emptyset$ iff the start symbol never gets marked.

**III is undecidable.** This is the universality problem for CFGs: does $G$ generate every string over its alphabet?
- It is undecidable, which is proved by reduction from PCP or by encoding the invalid computation histories of a TM as a CFL.
- Universality is decidable only for restricted classes, such as regular languages or deterministic CFLs.

**IV is undecidable.** This is the acceptance (membership) problem $A_{TM}$, which is undecidable by the standard diagonal argument. It is only semi-decidable, by simulating $M$ on $w$.

The undecidable problems are III and IV.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v2_6.7.1.q:
Consider the DFA $M$ and NFA $M_2$ as defined below. Let the language accepted by machine $M$ be $L$. What language machine $M_2$ accepts, if

- (i) $F2 = A$?
- (ii) $F2 = B$?
- (iii) $F2 = C$?
- (iv) $F2 = D$?

- $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$
- $M_2 = (Q2, \Sigma, \delta_2, q_{00}, F2)$

Where,

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q2 &= (Q \times Q \times Q) \cup \{q_{00}\}\\
\delta_2(q_{00}, \epsilon) &= \{\langle q_0, q, q\rangle \mid q \in Q\}\\
\delta_2(\langle p, q, r\rangle, \sigma) &= \langle \delta(p, \sigma), \delta(q, \sigma), r\rangle \quad \text{for all } p, q, r \in Q \text{ and } \sigma \in \Sigma\\
A &= \{\langle p, q, r\rangle \mid p \in F;\ q, r \in Q\}\\
B &= \{\langle p, q, r\rangle \mid q \in F;\ p, r \in Q\}\\
C &= \{\langle p, q, r\rangle \mid p, q, r \in Q;\ \exists s \in \Sigma^*,\ \delta(p, s) \in F\}\\
D &= \{\langle p, q, r\rangle \mid p, q \in Q;\ r \in F\}
\end{aligned}
$$
go_v2_6.7.1.e:
**Key idea.** After its single $\epsilon$-move, $M_2$ guesses a state $q \in Q$ and enters $\langle q_0, q, q\rangle$. From then on it runs three tracks in lock-step: track 1 simulates $M$ from $q_0$, track 2 simulates $M$ from the guessed state $q$, and track 3 never changes (it just remembers $q$). So after reading $w$ the NFA is in

$$\langle \hat\delta(q_0, w),\ \hat\delta(q, w),\ q\rangle, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad w \in L(M_2) \iff \exists q \in Q:\ \langle \hat\delta(q_0,w), \hat\delta(q,w), q\rangle \in F2 .$$

($q_{00} \notin F2$, so nothing is accepted without the $\epsilon$-move.)

**(i) $F2 = A$:** the condition is $\hat\delta(q_0, w) \in F$, independent of the guess. So $L(M_2) = L$.

**(ii) $F2 = B$:** the condition is $\hat\delta(q, w) \in F$ for some $q$. If $q = \hat\delta(q_0, x)$, this says exactly $xw \in L$. Hence $L(M_2) = \{w \mid \exists x \in \Sigma^*:\ xw \in L\}$, the set of all **suffixes** of strings in $L$. (This assumes every state of $M$ is reachable; in general it is $\{w \mid \exists q \in Q,\ \hat\delta(q, w) \in F\}$.)

**(iii) $F2 = C$:** the condition is that some final state can be reached from $p = \hat\delta(q_0, w)$, i.e. $\exists s:\ \hat\delta(q_0, ws) \in F \iff ws \in L$. So $L(M_2) = \{w \mid \exists s \in \Sigma^*:\ ws \in L\}$, the set of all **prefixes** of strings in $L$.

**(iv) $F2 = D$:** the condition is that the remembered guess satisfies $q \in F$, which does not depend on $w$ at all. If $F \neq \emptyset$, guess some $q \in F$; then every string (including $\epsilon$) is accepted, so $L(M_2) = \Sigma^*$. If $F = \emptyset$, then $L(M_2) = \emptyset$.

**Answer: (i) $L$; (ii) $\mathrm{Suffix}(L)$; (iii) $\mathrm{Prefix}(L)$; (iv) $\Sigma^*$ (or $\emptyset$ if $F = \emptyset$)**

go_v2_6.7.2.q: Let $L$ be the language of all binary strings in which the third symbol from the right is a $1$. Give a non-deterministic finite automaton that recognizes $L$. How many states does the minimized equivalent deterministic finite automaton have? Justify your answer briefly?
go_v2_6.7.2.e:
**NFA.** $L = (0+1)^*\,1\,(0+1)(0+1)$. The NFA loops in $q_0$ and nondeterministically guesses which $1$ is the third symbol from the right:

| State | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ | $\{q_0\}$ | $\{q_0, q_1\}$ |
| $q_1$ | $\{q_2\}$ | $\{q_2\}$ |
| $q_2$ | $\{q_3\}$ | $\{q_3\}$ |
| $q_3$ (final) | $\emptyset$ | $\emptyset$ |

**Minimized DFA: 8 states.** A DFA only needs to remember the last three symbols read. Use the states $b_1b_2b_3 \in \{0,1\}^3$, with the start state $000$ (shorter inputs act as if padded with leading 0's). The transitions are $b_1b_2b_3 \xrightarrow{c} b_2b_3c$, and the accepting states are those with $b_1 = 1$ ($100, 101, 110, 111$). That is 8 states.

**Why no DFA can use fewer (Myhill–Nerode).** Take two different 3-bit strings $x \neq y$. Let $i$ be the first position from the left where they differ, say $x_i = 1$ and $y_i = 0$. Appending $z = 0^{\,i-1}$ makes position $i$ the third symbol from the right, so $xz \in L$ but $yz \notin L$. So all 8 strings of length 3 are pairwise distinguishable, and each needs its own state.

In general, "the $n$-th symbol from the right is 1" needs $2^n$ DFA states, although an $(n+1)$-state NFA is enough.

**Answer: 4-state NFA as above; the minimized DFA has 8 states**

go_v2_6.7.3.q: Draw the state transition of a deterministic finite state automaton which accepts all strings from the alphabet $\{a, b\}$, such that no string has $3$ consecutive occurrences of the letter $b$.
go_v2_6.7.3.e:
**Key idea.** Remember how many $b$'s have just been read in a row (0, 1 or 2). A third consecutive $b$ sends the machine to a dead state.

| State | Meaning | a | b |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ (final) | no trailing $b$ | $q_0$ | $q_1$ |
| $q_1$ (final) | one trailing $b$ | $q_0$ | $q_2$ |
| $q_2$ (final) | two trailing $b$'s | $q_0$ | $q_3$ |
| $q_3$ (dead) | $bbb$ has occurred | $q_3$ | $q_3$ |

As a diagram: $q_0 \xrightarrow{b} q_1 \xrightarrow{b} q_2 \xrightarrow{b} q_3$. Every $a$ from $q_0$, $q_1$ or $q_2$ goes back to $q_0$, and $q_3$ loops on both $a$ and $b$. The final states are $q_0, q_1, q_2$. So $\epsilon$, $b$, $bb$ and $abbab$ are accepted, while $abbba$ is rejected.

**The DFA is minimal.** $q_3$ is the only non-final state. The final states are told apart by suffixes: $bb$ is accepted from $q_0$ but not from $q_1$, and $b$ is accepted from $q_0$ and $q_1$ but not from $q_2$.

An equivalent regular expression is $(a + ba + bba)^*(\epsilon + b + bb)$.

**Answer: 4-state DFA ($q_0, q_1, q_2$ accepting, $q_3$ dead)**

**What the machines accept.** $M_1$ alternates between $A$ and $B$ on every symbol and $A$ is final, so $L_1 = ((0+1)(0+1))^*$, the binary strings of even length. In $M_2$, the trap state $E$ is entered by reading $a$ after a $b$, and $C, D$ are final, so $L_2 = a^*b^*$. Note that $\varepsilon \in L_1$ and $\varepsilon \in L_2$.

**(a) $L_1.L_2$.** Add one $\varepsilon$-edge $A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} C$, from the final state of $M_1$ to the start state of $M_2$. The start state is still $A$. $A$ is no longer final, and the final states are $C$ and $D$.

| State | 0 | 1 | a | b | $\varepsilon$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\to A$ | $B$ | $B$ | – | – | $C$ |
| $B$ | $A$ | $A$ | – | – | – |
| $C$ (final) | – | – | $C$ | $D$ | – |
| $D$ (final) | – | – | $E$ | $D$ | – |
| $E$ | – | – | $E$ | $E$ | – |

Why it works: an accepting path stays in $M_1$ until it takes the only bridge $A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} C$. The part read before the bridge leads from $A$ back to $A$, so it is in $L_1$. The rest leads from $C$ to $C$ or $D$, so it is in $L_2$. (Keeping $A$ final would also be harmless here, because $\varepsilon \in L_2$ gives $L_1 \subseteq L_1L_2$.)

**(b) $(L_1.L_2)^*$.** Keep the machine from (a) and add $\varepsilon$-edges from its final states back to the start: $C \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} A$ and $D \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} A$. The start state is still $A$ and the final states are still $C$ and $D$. The $\varepsilon$-edges are now $A \to C$, $C \to A$ and $D \to A$.

Why it works: an accepting path is a sequence of rounds. In each round the machine goes from $A$ back to $A$ inside $M_1$ (reading a string of $L_1$), crosses $A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} C$, and goes from $C$ to $C$ or $D$ inside $M_2$ (reading a string of $L_2$). Then it either stops in a final state or returns to $A$ by a new $\varepsilon$-edge. So exactly $(L_1L_2)^+$ is accepted. Since $\varepsilon \in L_1L_2$ (the path $A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} C$ already accepts it), $(L_1L_2)^+ = (L_1L_2)^*$.

No new start state is needed. $A$ is never made final, so its incoming $0/1$ edges from $B$ cannot let any unwanted string be accepted.

**Answer: (a) add the $\varepsilon$-edge $A \to C$ (final states $C, D$); (b) also add the $\varepsilon$-edges $C \to A$ and $D \to A$**

go_v2_6.7.5.q:
Given that $L$ is a language accepted by a finite state machine, show that $L^P$ and $L^R$ are also accepted by some finite state machines, where

$L^P = \{s \mid ss' \in L \text{ some string } s'\}$

$L^R = \{s \mid s \text{ obtained by reversing some string in } L\}$
go_v2_6.7.5.e:
Let $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ be a DFA with $L(M) = L$.

**$L^P$ (prefixes).** Keep $M$ unchanged except for its final states:

$$M^P = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F'), \qquad F' = \{q \in Q \mid \exists s' \in \Sigma^*:\ \hat\delta(q, s') \in F\}.$$

$F'$ is the set of states from which some final state can be reached. It is computable by a graph search backwards from $F$, and it contains $F$. Correctness:

$$s \in L(M^P) \iff \hat\delta(q_0, s) \in F' \iff \exists s':\ \hat\delta(q_0, ss') \in F \iff \exists s':\ ss' \in L \iff s \in L^P .$$

So $M^P$ is a finite automaton accepting $L^P$.

**$L^R$ (reversal).** Build an NFA $N$ by running $M$ backwards:
- the states are $Q \cup \{q_s\}$, where $q_s$ is a new start state;
- add $q_s \xrightarrow{\epsilon} f$ for every $f \in F$;
- for every transition $\delta(p, a) = q$ of $M$, add the reversed transition $q \xrightarrow{a} p$;
- the only final state is $q_0$.

A path in $N$ reading $s = a_1a_2\cdots a_n$ goes $q_s \to f \to \cdots \to q_0$. Such a path exists exactly when $M$ has a path from $q_0$ reading $a_n\cdots a_2a_1$ that ends in $f \in F$, i.e. when $s^R \in L$. Hence $L(N) = L^R$. $N$ is a finite automaton (nondeterministic, with $\epsilon$-moves), and the subset construction gives an equivalent DFA. So $L^R$ is accepted by a finite state machine.

(If $F = \emptyset$ then $L = L^P = L^R = \emptyset$, and both constructions still work.)

**Answer: $L^P$ — same DFA with $F' = \{q : q \text{ can reach } F\}$; $L^R$ — reversed NFA starting from $F$ and accepting at $q_0$**

go_v2_6.7.7.q:
Construct DFA's for the following languages:

A. $L = \{w \mid w \in \{a, b\}^*,\ w \text{ has baab as a substring}\}$

B. $L = \{w \mid w \in \{a, b\}^*,\ w \text{ has an odd number of a's and an odd number of b's}\}$
go_v2_6.7.7.e:
**(A) Substring $baab$.** State $q_i$ means that the longest suffix of the input read so far which is also a prefix of $baab$ has length $i$. $q_4$ means $baab$ has already appeared; it is a final trap state.

| State | Matched so far | a | b |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ | – | $q_0$ | $q_1$ |
| $q_1$ | $b$ | $q_2$ | $q_1$ |
| $q_2$ | $ba$ | $q_3$ | $q_1$ |
| $q_3$ | $baa$ | $q_0$ | $q_4$ |
| $q_4$ (final) | $baab$ | $q_4$ | $q_4$ |

The fall-back moves work like this. From $q_1$ on $b$, "$bb$" still ends in $b$, so the machine stays in $q_1$. From $q_2$ on $b$, "$bab$" ends in $b$, so it goes to $q_1$. From $q_3$ on $a$, no suffix of "$baaa$" starts $baab$, so it goes to $q_0$.

The DFA is minimal: the shortest accepted continuation from $q_i$ has length $4 - i$, so all five states are distinguishable.

**(B) Odd number of $a$'s and odd number of $b$'s.** Each state records the two parities: $EE$ (start), $OE$, $EO$ and $OO$ (final), where the first letter is the parity of $a$'s and the second the parity of $b$'s. Reading $a$ flips the first parity and reading $b$ flips the second.

| State | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $\to EE$ | $OE$ | $EO$ |
| $OE$ | $EE$ | $OO$ |
| $EO$ | $OO$ | $EE$ |
| $OO$ (final) | $EO$ | $OE$ |

For example, $ab$ and $babbaa$ are accepted, while $aab$ is rejected. This DFA is also minimal, since each state needs a different shortest accepted continuation: $\epsilon$, $a$, $b$ or $ab$.

**Answer: (A) 5-state DFA with final trap state $q_4$; (B) 4-state parity DFA with final state $OO$**

A. Give an NFA for this purpose

B. Give a DFA for this purpose

**(A) NFA with 4 states.** $q_0$ loops on both symbols and guesses where the final $abb$ begins:

| State | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ | $\{q_0, q_1\}$ | $\{q_0\}$ |
| $q_1$ | $\emptyset$ | $\{q_2\}$ |
| $q_2$ | $\emptyset$ | $\{q_3\}$ |
| $q_3$ (final) | $\emptyset$ | $\emptyset$ |

**(B) DFA with 4 states.** The subset construction from $\{q_0\}$ reaches only $P_0 = \{q_0\}$, $P_1 = \{q_0, q_1\}$, $P_2 = \{q_0, q_2\}$ and $P_3 = \{q_0, q_3\}$. In words, $P_1$ means the input ends in $a$, $P_2$ that it ends in $ab$, and $P_3$ that it ends in $abb$.

| State | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $\to P_0$ | $P_1$ | $P_0$ |
| $P_1$ | $P_1$ | $P_2$ |
| $P_2$ | $P_1$ | $P_3$ |
| $P_3$ (final) | $P_1$ | $P_0$ |

The DFA is minimal. $P_3$ is the only final state, the suffix $b$ separates $P_2$ from $P_0$ and $P_1$, and the suffix $bb$ separates $P_1$ from $P_0$.

**Answer: NFA $q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_1 \xrightarrow{b} q_2 \xrightarrow{b} q_3$ with an $a,b$ loop on $q_0$; DFA as tabulated with final state $P_3$**

go_v2_6.7.14.q:
The following diagram represents a finite state machine which takes as input a binary number from the least significant bit.

Figure (Mealy machine; edge labels are input/output; start state $Q_0$):

- $Q_0 \xrightarrow{0/0} Q_0$ (self-loop)
- $Q_0 \xrightarrow{1/1} Q_1$
- $Q_1 \xrightarrow{0/1} Q_1$ (self-loop)
- $Q_1 \xrightarrow{1/0} Q_1$ (self-loop)

Which of the following is TRUE?
o: It computes $1$'s complement of the input number
It computes $2$'s complement of the input number
go_v2_6.7.14.e:
**Key idea.** In $Q_0$ the bits are copied unchanged ($0/0$) up to the first $1$. That $1$ is also copied ($1/1$) and moves the machine to $Q_1$. In $Q_1$ every later bit is inverted ($0/1$, $1/0$). Copying from the LSB up to and including the first $1$, then complementing everything after it, is exactly the shortcut for the 2's complement.

**Example:** input $0110$ (six) is fed LSB first as $0, 1, 1, 0$. The outputs are $0$ (copy), $1$ (copy, go to $Q_1$), $0$ (inverted), $1$ (inverted). Read MSB first, the output is $1010$, and $1010 = 16 - 6$ is the 4-bit 2's complement of $0110$.

The other options would give: 1's complement $1001$, increment $0111$, decrement $0101$. None of these matches the machine's output.

Edge case: an all-zero input stays in $Q_0$ and outputs all zeros. That is also correct, since the 2's complement of 0 is 0.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v2_6.7.24.e:
**Key idea.** For an $\epsilon$-NFA, $\hat\delta(q, w)$ starts from the $\epsilon$-closure of $q$. After each input symbol, take all moves on that symbol and then the $\epsilon$-closure of the result.

**$\epsilon$-closures.** The $\epsilon$-edges are $q_0 \to q_2$, $q_1 \to q_2$ and $q_2 \to q_0$, so
- $E(q_0) = \{q_0, q_2\}$
- $E(q_1) = \{q_0, q_1, q_2\}$
- $E(q_2) = \{q_0, q_2\}$
- $E(q_3) = \{q_3\}$

1. Start: $E(q_2) = \{q_0, q_2\}$.
2. Read $a$: $\delta(q_0, a) \cup \delta(q_2, a) = \{q_1\}$. The closure is $\{q_0, q_1, q_2\}$.
3. Read $b$: $\delta(q_0, b) \cup \delta(q_1, b) \cup \delta(q_2, b) = \{q_0\} \cup \{q_3\} \cup \emptyset = \{q_0, q_3\}$. The closure is $\{q_0, q_2, q_3\}$.
4. Read $a$: $\delta(q_0, a) \cup \delta(q_2, a) \cup \delta(q_3, a) = \{q_1\}$. The closure is $\{q_0, q_1, q_2\}$.

So $\hat\delta(q_2, aba) = \{q_0, q_1, q_2\}$.

$K = \{A, B\}$, $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$, $s = A$, $F = \{B\}$,
$\sigma(A, a) = A$, $\sigma(A, b) = B$, $\sigma(B, a) = B$ and $\sigma(B, b) = A$

o: $\{A \rightarrow aB,\ A \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow aA,\ B \rightarrow \epsilon\}$
$\{A \rightarrow aA,\ A \rightarrow bB,\ B \rightarrow aB,\ B \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow \epsilon\}$
$\{A \rightarrow bB,\ A \rightarrow aB,\ B \rightarrow aA,\ B \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow \epsilon\}$
$\{A \rightarrow aA,\ A \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow aB,\ B \rightarrow bA,\ A \rightarrow \epsilon\}$
go_v2_6.7.33.e:
**Key idea.** A DFA turns into a right-linear grammar as follows: each transition $\sigma(X, c) = Y$ gives the rule $X \to cY$, each final state $X$ gives $X \to \epsilon$, and the start state is the start symbol.

- $\sigma(A, a) = A \Rightarrow A \to aA$
- $\sigma(A, b) = B \Rightarrow A \to bB$
- $\sigma(B, a) = B \Rightarrow B \to aB$
- $\sigma(B, b) = A \Rightarrow B \to bA$
- $B \in F \Rightarrow B \to \epsilon$

- (C) also has $A \to aB$ and $B \to \epsilon$, so it generates $a$ as well.
- (D) has $A \to \epsilon$ even though $A$ is not final, and $B$ can never be reached from $A$. It generates every string, including $\epsilon$.

Consider the non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) shown in the figure.

Figure (start state $X$; no accepting state marked):

| State | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to X$ | $\{Y, Z\}$ | $\{X\}$ |
| $Y$ | $\{Y, Z\}$ | $\emptyset$ |
| $Z$ | $\{X\}$ | $\{Y, Z\}$ |

| Subset | on 0 | on 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\{X\}$ | $\{Y, Z\}$ | $\{X\}$ |
| $\{Y, Z\}$ | $\{Y, Z\} \cup \{X\} = \{X, Y, Z\}$ | $\emptyset \cup \{Y, Z\} = \{Y, Z\}$ |
| $\{X, Y, Z\}$ | $\{X, Y, Z\}$ | $\{X, Y, Z\}$ |

Because the languages are equal, neither proper-subset option (B) nor (C) holds, and (D) is wrong.

Consider the regular grammar:

- $S \rightarrow Xa \mid Ya$
- $X \rightarrow Za$
- $Z \rightarrow Sa \mid \epsilon$
- $Y \rightarrow Wa$
- $W \rightarrow Sa$

where $S$ is the starting symbol, the set of terminals is $\{a\}$ and the set of non-terminals is $\{S, W, X, Y, Z\}$.

We wish to construct a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) to recognize the same language. What is the minimum number of states required for the DFA?
go_v2_6.7.35.e:
**Key idea.** Eliminate the non-terminals to find the language. It turns out to be a unary language with period 3.

- From $Z \to Sa \mid \epsilon$ and $X \to Za$: $X \Rightarrow Saa$ or $X \Rightarrow a$.
- From $W \to Sa$ and $Y \to Wa$: $Y \Rightarrow Saa$.
- Substituting into $S \to Xa \mid Ya$ gives $S \to Saaa \mid aa$. The $Y$ branch adds nothing new.

So $L = aa(aaa)^* = \{a^n \mid n \equiv 2 \pmod 3\} = \{a^2, a^5, a^8, \dots\}$.

**Minimum DFA:** a 3-state cycle that counts $n \bmod 3$: $q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_1 \xrightarrow{a} q_2 \xrightarrow{a} q_0$, with start state $q_0$ and final state $q_2$. No dead state is needed. The three states are pairwise distinguishable, since the shortest accepted continuations from $q_0$, $q_1$ and $q_2$ are $aa$, $a$ and $\epsilon$. Two states are not enough, because they cannot track $n \bmod 3$.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v2_6.9.2.q: What is the type of the language $L$, where $L = \{a^n b^n \mid 0 < n < 327\text{-th prime number}\}$
go_v2_6.9.2.e:
**Key idea:** the upper bound on $n$ is a fixed constant. So $L$ contains only finitely many strings, and every finite language is regular.

The 327-th prime is a specific number ($2179$), so
$$L = \{ab,\ a^2b^2,\ \dots,\ a^{2178}b^{2178}\},$$
a set of $2178$ strings. A finite language is regular. Its regular expression is simply the union of its finitely many strings. Equivalently, a DFA can remember the whole input up to length $2\cdot 2178$ and move to a dead state beyond that. Hence $L$ is **regular (Chomsky Type 3)**, and therefore also context-free, context-sensitive and recursive.

Contrast this with the unbounded language $\{a^nb^n \mid n \ge 1\}$, which is context-free but not regular. Its pumping-lemma proof needs a string $a^pb^p$ with $p$ larger than the pumping length, and that is impossible here because $n$ is bounded. When the counts are bounded, matching the number of $a$'s and $b$'s needs only a finite amount of memory.

**Answer: $L$ is regular (Type 3), since it is finite.**

go_v2_6.9.3.q: Show that the Turing machines, which have a read only input tape and constant size work tape, recognize precisely the class of regular languages.
go_v2_6.9.3.e:
Let $M$ have:
- a finite control $Q$;
- a read-only input tape holding $\vdash w \dashv$ (with endmarkers), whose head may move both ways;
- a work tape of exactly $k$ cells over an alphabet $\Gamma$, where $k$ does not depend on the input.

**1. Every regular language is recognised by such a machine.** Take a DFA $A=(P,\Sigma,\delta,p_0,F)$. Let $M$ move its input head one cell right per step, change state according to $\delta$, and never use the work tape. When it reaches $\dashv$, it accepts iff its state is in $F$. Then $L(M)=L(A)$.

**2. Every such machine accepts a regular language.**

*(a) Fold the work tape into the finite control.* At any moment the work tape is fully described by its contents ($|\Gamma|^k$ possibilities) and the position of its head ($k$ possibilities). Use the new state set
$$Q' = Q \times \Gamma^k \times \{1,\dots,k\},$$
which is finite, of size $|Q|\cdot|\Gamma|^k\cdot k$. A machine with states $Q'$ and only the read-only two-way input head simulates $M$ step by step. So $M$ is equivalent to a **two-way DFA** $D$ with state set $Q'$. We may assume $D$ accepts only by halting on $\dashv$: whenever it would accept, it first walks right to $\dashv$.

*(b) Two-way DFAs accept only regular languages (Shepherdson).* For a string $x$, define a function $T_x : Q' \cup \{\bullet\} \to Q' \cup \{\bot\}$:
- $T_x(\bullet)$ is the state in which $D$, started normally at the left end, first moves off the right end of $\vdash x$. It is $\bot$ if that never happens.
- For a state $p$, $T_x(p)$ is the state in which $D$ next moves off the right end of $\vdash x$, after entering the last cell of $\vdash x$ from the right in state $p$. It is $\bot$ if $D$ never comes out.

$D$ can never leave on the left, because of $\vdash$.

Suppose $T_x = T_y$, and let $z$ be any string. Compare the runs of $D$ on $\vdash xz\dashv$ and on $\vdash yz\dashv$:
- Both leave the prefix in the same state $T_x(\bullet) = T_y(\bullet)$.
- They then move identically inside $z$ until they re-enter the prefix, both in the same state $p$.
- They come out again in the same state $T_x(p) = T_y(p)$, and so on.
- If one gets stuck inside the prefix ($\bot$), so does the other.

Hence $xz \in L(D) \iff yz \in L(D)$, so $x$ and $y$ are Myhill–Nerode equivalent. There are at most $(|Q'|+1)^{|Q'|+1}$ different functions $T_x$. So the Myhill–Nerode relation of $L(D)$ has finite index, and $L(D)$ is regular.

**Conclusion.** A read-only input tape cannot be used as extra storage, and a work tape of constant size adds only finitely many configurations. Such a machine therefore has only finite memory. By parts 1 and 2, these machines recognise exactly the regular languages.

**Answer: Folding the constant-size work tape into the finite control turns the machine into a two-way DFA, and two-way DFAs accept exactly the regular languages.**

go_v2_6.9.4.q:
A. Given a set:
$$S = \{x \mid \text{there is an } x\text{-block of 5's in the decimal expansion of } \pi\}$$
(Note: $x$-block is a maximal block of $x$ successive 5's)

Which of the following statements is true with respect to $S$? No reason to be given for the answer.

i. $S$ is regular
ii. $S$ is recursively enumerable
iii. $S$ is not recursively enumerable
iv. $S$ is recursive

B. Given that a language $L_1$ is regular and that the language $L_1 \cup L_2$ is regular, is the language $L_2$ always regular? Prove your answer.
go_v2_6.9.4.e:
**Part A.**
- ***(ii) holds.*** The digits of $\pi$ are computable: an algorithm can print the $n$-th digit for any $n$. To semi-decide whether $x \in S$, generate the digits one by one and track the runs of 5's. A run is known to be maximal once a non-5 digit follows it, and every run does end because $\pi$ is irrational. Accept as soon as a maximal run of exactly $x$ fives has been completed. This procedure halts exactly when $x \in S$, so $S$ is recursively enumerable. Hence (iii) is false.
- ***(i) and (iv) cannot be asserted.*** To reject an $x \notin S$, one would have to know that no maximal run of exactly $x$ fives occurs anywhere in the infinite expansion, and no method for that is known. If $\pi$ is normal (widely believed, but unproved), then every pattern $d\,5^x d'$ with $d, d' \neq 5$ occurs. In that case $S=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$, which is recursive and even regular. Since this is an open problem, (i) and (iv) are not known to be true.
- ***Why "maximal" matters.*** Suppose "$x$-block" meant "at least $x$ successive 5's". Then $S$ would be either all of $\mathbb{N}$ or $\{1,\dots,k\}$ for some $k$. Either way it would be recursive (indeed regular), even though we would not know which case holds. With exact, maximal blocks this argument no longer works.

So the statement that can be asserted with certainty is **(ii)**.

**Part B. No.** Let $\Sigma = \{a,b\}$, $L_1 = \Sigma^*$ (regular) and $L_2 = \{a^nb^n \mid n \ge 0\}$. Then $L_1 \cup L_2 = \Sigma^*$ is regular.

$L_2$ is not regular. Suppose it were, with pumping length $p$. Write $a^pb^p = uvw$ with $|uv| \le p$ and $|v| \ge 1$. Then $v = a^t$ with $t \ge 1$, and $uv^2w = a^{p+t}b^p \notin L_2$, a contradiction.

So "$L_1$ regular and $L_1 \cup L_2$ regular" does **not** force $L_2$ to be regular, because a large regular $L_1$ can absorb any $L_2$. The same holds for intersection: $L_1 = \emptyset$ makes $L_1 \cap L_2 = \emptyset$ regular for every $L_2$.

**Answer: A: (ii) only ($S$ is recursively enumerable). B: No; $L_1=\Sigma^*$, $L_2=\{a^nb^n\}$ is a counterexample.**
go_v2_6.9.4.note: Part A: only (ii) is provable; (i) and (iv) depend on open questions about π (both would hold if π were normal), so the expected answer is debatable. Part B overlaps es_jaAxrLzd3VUh890k, which asks the same thing with L1 ∩ L2 instead of L1 ∪ L2.

go_v2_6.9.20.q:
Consider the context-free grammars over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$ given below. $S$ and $T$ are non-terminals.

$G_1: S \rightarrow aSb \mid T,\ T \rightarrow cT \mid \epsilon$

$G_2: S \rightarrow bSa \mid T,\ T \rightarrow cT \mid \epsilon$

The language $L(G_1) \cap L(G_2)$ is
go_v2_6.9.20.e:
**The two languages:**
$$L(G_1) = \{a^n c^m b^n \mid n, m \ge 0\}, \qquad L(G_2) = \{b^n c^m a^n \mid n, m \ge 0\}.$$

**Their intersection:** let $w$ belong to both languages.
- If $w \in L(G_1)$ uses $n \ge 1$, then $w$ starts with $a$. No string of $L(G_2)$ starts with $a$: each one starts with $b$ (when $n \ge 1$) or is $c^m$. So $n = 0$ on the $G_1$ side.
- In the same way, a string of $L(G_2)$ with $n \ge 1$ starts with $b$, and no string of $L(G_1)$ does. So $n = 0$ on the $G_2$ side too.

Hence only the middle part survives:
$$L(G_1) \cap L(G_2) = \{c^m \mid m \ge 0\} = c^*.$$

This is the regular expression $c^*$, which is infinite and regular.
- (A) fails because the set is not finite.
- (C) fails because the set is regular.
- (D) fails because the set is context-free.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v2_6.9.21.q:
Consider the following languages.

- $L_1 = \{a^p \mid p \text{ is a prime number}\}$
- $L_2 = \{a^n b^m c^{2m} \mid n \geq 0, m \geq 0\}$
- $L_3 = \{a^n b^n c^{2n} \mid n \geq 0\}$
- $L_4 = \{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 1\}$

Which of the following are CORRECT?

I. $L_1$ is context free but not regular

II. $L_2$ is not context free

III. $L_3$ is not context free but recursive

IV. $L_4$ is deterministic context free
go_v2_6.9.21.e:
**I is false.** $L_1$ is not even context-free. Over a one-letter alphabet every CFL is regular (Parikh's theorem), so it is enough to show that $L_1$ is not regular.
- Pump $a^p$, where $p$ is a prime at least the pumping length, using a pumped part of length $k \ge 1$.
- The pumped strings $xy^iz$ have length $p + (i-1)k$.
- Taking $i = p+1$ gives length $p(1+k)$, which is composite.

**II is false.** $L_2$ is context-free: $S \to AB,\ A \to aA \mid \epsilon,\ B \to bBcc \mid \epsilon$. Only the two counts $m$ and $2m$ have to match, and one stack can do that.

**III is true.** $L_3$ needs three counts to agree ($n$, $n$ and $2n$).
- Pumping $a^p b^p c^{2p}$ changes at most two of the blocks, so $L_3$ is not a CFL.
- It is plainly decidable: count the symbols and compare. So it is recursive.

**IV is true.** A DPDA for $L_4$ works deterministically:
- it pushes each $a$;
- it pops one $a$ for each $b$;
- it accepts on reaching the bottom marker after at least one $b$.

So $L_4$ is a DCFL.

The correct statements are III and IV.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v2_6.9.29.q: Let $L$ be a regular language and $M$ be a context-free language, both over the alphabet $\Sigma$. Let $L^c$ and $M^c$ denote the complements of $L$ and $M$ respectively. Which of the following statements about the language $L^c \cup M^c$ is TRUE?
o: It is necessarily regular but not necessarily context-free.
go_v2_6.9.29.e:
**Key idea:** by De Morgan, $L^c \cup M^c = (L \cap M)^c$. Here $L \cap M$ is context-free, because CFLs are closed under intersection with regular sets. But CFLs are **not** closed under complement, so nothing forces the result to be regular, context-free, or non-regular.

Test each option with a choice of $L$ and $M$:
- **Option (B) fails.** Take $L = \Sigma^*$, so $L^c = \emptyset$ and the union is just $M^c$. Let $M = \overline{\{a^nb^nc^n \mid n \ge 0\}}$, which is a CFL. Then $M^c = \{a^nb^nc^n\}$ is not context-free.
- **Option (A) fails.** It is self-contradictory, since every regular language is context-free. The same example also shows the union need not be regular.
- **Option (C) fails.** Take $M = \Sigma^*$, so $M^c = \emptyset$. The union is $L^c$, which is regular.

No option holds in general.

**Answer: (D)**

o: context-free but its complement is not context-free
go_v2_6.9.30.e:
**Key idea:** because $n$ is bounded by the constant $10^6$, the language contains exactly $10^6$ strings: $012,\ 001122,\ \dots,\ 0^{10^6}1^{10^6}2^{10^6}$. Every **finite** language is regular, since it is the union of finitely many single strings.

The unbounded language $\{0^n1^n2^n \mid n \ge 1\}$ is not even context-free. That proof needs arbitrarily large $n$, which this language does not have.

- (B) is false because the language *is* regular.
- (C) is false because the complement of a regular language is regular, hence context-free.

**Option B is true.**
- Every word of $L_1$ contains a $c$ and no word of $L_2$ does, so $L_1 \cap L_2 = \varnothing$.
- $L_1$ is not regular. If it were, then $L_1 \cap a^*b^*c = \{a^n b^n c \mid n \ge 0\}$ would also be regular. Removing the final $c$ (a right quotient by $c$) would then make $\{a^n b^n\}$ regular, which is false.

**The other options fail.**
- (A) $L_1$ is a CFL: $S \to XC,\ X \to aXb \mid \epsilon,\ C \to cC \mid c$.
- (C) CFLs are closed under union, so $L_1 \cup L_2$ is a CFL.
- (D) $L_2$ is deterministic context-free. A DPDA pushes two symbols for every $a$ and pops one for every $b$. It accepts when the stack is back at the bottom marker. So "no DPDA accepts $L_2$" is false.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v2_6.11.2.q: Construct a finite state machine with minimum number of states, accepting all strings over $(a, b)$ such that the number of $a$'s is divisible by two and the number of $b$'s is divisible by three.
go_v2_6.11.2.e:
**Key idea.** Track two counters at once: $i = (\text{number of } a\text{'s}) \bmod 2$ and $j = (\text{number of } b\text{'s}) \bmod 3$. This is the product of a 2-state counter and a 3-state counter, so it has $2 \times 3 = 6$ states. Reading $a$ maps $(i, j) \mapsto ((i+1) \bmod 2,\ j)$, and reading $b$ maps $(i, j) \mapsto (i,\ (j+1) \bmod 3)$.

| State | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $\to (0,0)$ (final) | $(1,0)$ | $(0,1)$ |
| $(0,1)$ | $(1,1)$ | $(0,2)$ |
| $(0,2)$ | $(1,2)$ | $(0,0)$ |
| $(1,0)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,1)$ |
| $(1,1)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(1,2)$ |
| $(1,2)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(1,0)$ |

The start state and the only final state are both $(0,0)$. For example, $\epsilon$, $aa$, $bbb$ and $abbab$ are accepted, while $aab$ is not.

**Minimality.** Take any two distinct states $(i, j) \neq (i', j')$ and the suffix $z = a^{(2-i) \bmod 2}\, b^{(3-j) \bmod 3}$. From $(i, j)$ it leads to $(0, 0)$, so $z$ is accepted. From $(i', j')$ it leads to $((i'-i) \bmod 2,\ (j'-j) \bmod 3) \neq (0, 0)$, so $z$ is rejected. All 6 states are therefore pairwise distinguishable, and no DFA with fewer states exists.

**Answer: 6 states (as tabulated)**

go_v2_6.11.3.q:
Following is a state table for time finite state machine.

| Present State | Next State Output: Input-0 | Next State Output: Input-1 |
|---|---|---|
| A | B.1 | H.1 |
| B | F.1 | D.1 |
| C | D.0 | E.1 |
| D | C.0 | F.1 |
| E | D.1 | C.1 |
| F | C.1 | C.1 |
| G | C.1 | D.1 |
| H | C.0 | A.1 |

A. Find the equivalence partition on the states of the machine.

B. Give the state table for the minimal machine. (Use appropriate names for the equivalent states. For example if states $X$ and $Y$ are equivalent then use $XY$ as the name for the equivalent state in the minimal machine).
go_v2_6.11.3.e:
**Key idea.** Use partition refinement. Start from groups with identical outputs, then split any group whose members move to different groups, until nothing changes. (An entry such as B.1 means next state $B$, output 1.)

**(A) Equivalence partition.**

- **$P_1$ (by outputs on inputs 0 and 1):** $A, B, E, F, G$ have $(1,1)$; $C, D, H$ have $(0,1)$. So $P_1 = \{A,B,E,F,G\},\ \{C,D,H\}$. Call these blocks $X$ and $Y$.
- **$P_2$:** the next states map to blocks as follows. $A \to (B,H) = (X,Y)$, $B \to (F,D) = (X,Y)$; $E \to (D,C)$, $F \to (C,C)$, $G \to (C,D)$, all $(Y,Y)$; $C \to (D,E)$, $D \to (C,F)$, $H \to (C,A)$, all $(Y,X)$. So $P_2 = \{A,B\},\ \{E,F,G\},\ \{C,D,H\}$.
- **$P_3$:** $A \to (B,H)$ lands in $(\{A,B\}, \{C,D,H\})$, but $B \to (F,D)$ lands in $(\{E,F,G\}, \{C,D,H\})$, so $A$ and $B$ split. $C \to (D,E)$ and $D \to (C,F)$ land in $(\{C,D,H\}, \{E,F,G\})$, but $H \to (C,A)$ lands in $(\{C,D,H\}, \{A,B\})$, so $H$ splits off. $E, F, G$ all still move into $(\{C,D,H\}, \{C,D,H\})$. So $P_3 = \{A\},\ \{B\},\ \{C,D\},\ \{E,F,G\},\ \{H\}$.
- **$P_4$:** $C \to (D,E)$ and $D \to (C,F)$ both land in $(CD, EFG)$. $E \to (D,C)$, $F \to (C,C)$ and $G \to (C,D)$ all land in $(CD, CD)$. Nothing splits, so $P_4 = P_3$ is final.

Equivalence partition: $\{A\},\ \{B\},\ \{C, D\},\ \{E, F, G\},\ \{H\}$.

**(B) Minimal machine (5 states):**

| Present State | Input 0 (Next, Output) | Input 1 (Next, Output) |
|---|---|---|
| $A$ | $B$, 1 | $H$, 1 |
| $B$ | $EFG$, 1 | $CD$, 1 |
| $CD$ | $CD$, 0 | $EFG$, 1 |
| $EFG$ | $CD$, 1 | $CD$, 1 |
| $H$ | $CD$, 0 | $A$, 1 |

**Answer: (A) $\{A\}, \{B\}, \{C,D\}, \{E,F,G\}, \{H\}$; (B) the 5-state table above**

go_v2_6.11.5.q:
Design a deterministic finite state automaton (using minimum number of states) that recognizes the following language:

$L = \{w \in \{0, 1\}^* \mid w \text{ interpreted as binary number (ignoring the leading zeros) is divisible by five}\}.$
go_v2_6.11.5.e:
**Key idea.** If the bits read so far have value $v$, reading one more bit $b$ gives the value $2v + b$. Only $v \bmod 5$ matters for divisibility, so the states are the remainders $r = 0, \dots, 4$ with

$$\delta(q_r, b) = q_{(2r + b) \bmod 5}.$$

Leading zeros keep the machine in $q_0$, so they are ignored automatically.

| State (remainder) | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ (final) | $q_0$ | $q_1$ |
| $q_1$ | $q_2$ | $q_3$ |
| $q_2$ | $q_4$ | $q_0$ |
| $q_3$ | $q_1$ | $q_2$ |
| $q_4$ | $q_3$ | $q_4$ |

Example: $1010$ (ten) goes $q_0 \to q_1 \to q_2 \to q_0 \to q_0$ and is accepted. $111$ (seven) goes $q_0 \to q_1 \to q_3 \to q_2$ and is rejected.

**Minimality.** Take two different remainders $r \neq s$. Pick a 3-bit suffix $z$ whose value $v$ satisfies $8r + v \equiv 0 \pmod 5$. Such a $z$ exists because 3-bit values $0..7$ cover every residue. Then $z$ is accepted from $q_r$. From $q_s$ the remainder becomes $8s + v \equiv 8(s - r) \not\equiv 0$, because $5$ divides neither $8$ nor $s - r$. So the 5 states are pairwise distinguishable, and 5 is the minimum.

**Answer: 5 states (remainders 0–4; $q_0$ is both start and final)**

go_v2_6.11.20.q: Consider the language $L$ given by the regular expression $(a+b)^*b(a+b)$ over the alphabet $\{a, b\}$. The smallest number of states needed in a deterministic finite-state automaton (DFA) accepting $L$ is ____________ .
go_v2_6.11.20.e:
**Key idea.** $L$ is the set of strings whose **second-last** symbol is $b$. A DFA has to remember the last two symbols it has read, and all four possibilities turn out to be distinguishable.

Name the states after the last two symbols. The start state behaves like $aa$, because no $b$ has been read yet. Likewise a lone $a$ behaves like $aa$, and a lone $b$ behaves like $ab$.

| State | Last two symbols | on $a$ | on $b$ | Final? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $q_{aa}$ (start) | $aa$ (or no $b$ yet) | $q_{aa}$ | $q_{ab}$ | no |
| $q_{ab}$ | $ab$ | $q_{ba}$ | $q_{bb}$ | no |
| $q_{ba}$ | $ba$ | $q_{aa}$ | $q_{ab}$ | yes |
| $q_{bb}$ | $bb$ | $q_{ba}$ | $q_{bb}$ | yes |

No two of these states can be merged:
- Any final state and any non-final state are separated by $\epsilon$.
- $q_{aa}$ and $q_{ab}$: append $a$. From $q_{aa}$ the last two become $aa$ (reject); from $q_{ab}$ they become $ba$ (accept).
- $q_{ba}$ and $q_{bb}$: append $a$. From $q_{ba}$ the last two become $aa$ (reject); from $q_{bb}$ they become $ba$ (accept).

So the minimal DFA has $4$ states. In general, "the $k$-th symbol from the end is $b$" needs $2^k$ states, and here $k = 2$.

**Answer: 4**

go_v2_6.11.21.q: The minimum possible number of states of a deterministic finite automaton that accepts the regular language $L = \{w_1 a w_2 \mid w_1, w_2 \in \{a,b\}^*,\ |w_1| = 2,\ |w_2| \geq 3\}$ is ______ .
go_v2_6.11.21.e:
**Key idea:** $L$ is the set of strings of length at least $6$ whose **third** symbol is $a$: two arbitrary symbols, then $a$, then at least three arbitrary symbols. A DFA must count the first two symbols, check the third, and then count up to three more symbols.

| State | on $a$ | on $b$ | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| $q_0$ (start) | $q_1$ | $q_1$ | nothing read |
| $q_1$ | $q_2$ | $q_2$ | 1 symbol read |
| $q_2$ | $q_3$ | $D$ | 2 symbols read; the 3rd must be $a$ |
| $q_3$ | $q_4$ | $q_4$ | need at least 3 more |
| $q_4$ | $q_5$ | $q_5$ | need at least 2 more |
| $q_5$ | $q_6$ | $q_6$ | need at least 1 more |
| $q_6$ (final) | $q_6$ | $q_6$ | accept anything further |
| $D$ (dead) | $D$ | $D$ | 3rd symbol was $b$ |

**No smaller DFA exists.** From each state, look at the length of the shortest continuation that leads to acceptance:

| $q_0$ | $q_1$ | $q_2$ | $q_3$ | $q_4$ | $q_5$ | $q_6$ | $D$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 | none |

Take two states where these lengths are $s < t$. A shortest accepted continuation of length $s$ from the first state is rejected from the second, because the second accepts nothing shorter than $t$. So all 8 states are pairwise distinguishable (8 Myhill–Nerode classes), and no DFA with fewer states can accept $L$.

**Answer: 8**

go_v2_6.11.25.q: Let $N$ be an NFA with $n$ states and let $M$ be the minimized DFA with $m$ states recognizing the same language. Which of the following in NECESSARILY true?
go_v2_6.11.25.e:
**Key idea.** The subset construction turns any $n$-state NFA into an equivalent DFA with at most $2^n$ states. The minimized DFA is no larger than any equivalent DFA, so $m \le 2^n$ always holds.

- (A) **Always true**, by the argument above.
- (B) False: an NFA can have more states than needed. A 2-state NFA for $a^*$ whose second state is unreachable has $n = 2$, while the minimal DFA has $m = 1$.
- (C) False: over $\{a\}$, the minimal DFA for $\{a, aa\}$ has two accept states, one after $a$ and one after $aa$. These cannot be merged, because $a\cdot a \in L$ but $aa\cdot a \notin L$.
- (D) False: $2^n$ is only the worst case. Over $\{a\}$, a 1-state NFA for $a^*$ gives $m = 1 \ne 2^1$.

**Answer: (A)**

go_v2_6.12.5.q: Which of the following pairs have **DIFFERENT** expressive power?
o: Deterministic finite automata (DFA) and Non-deterministic finite automata (NFA)
Deterministic push down automata (DPDA) and Non-deterministic push down automata (NPDA)
Deterministic single tape Turing machine and Non-deterministic single tape Turing machine
Single tape Turing machine and multi-tape Turing machine
go_v2_6.12.5.e:
**DFA vs NFA: same power.** The subset construction converts any NFA into an equivalent DFA, possibly with exponentially more states. Both recognise exactly the regular languages.

**DPDA vs NPDA: different power.** NPDAs accept all CFLs, but DPDAs accept only the deterministic CFLs, a proper subset.
- Example: $\{ww^R \mid w \in \{a,b\}^*\}$.
- An NPDA guesses where the middle of the input is.
- A DPDA cannot know where the middle is, so it cannot accept this language.

**Deterministic vs non-deterministic TM: same power.** A deterministic TM can search the non-deterministic computation tree breadth-first. It accepts the same language, only more slowly.

**Single-tape vs multi-tape TM: same power.** A single tape can hold all $k$ tapes as tracks, with the head positions marked. The simulation costs only a polynomial (quadratic) slowdown.

Only the PDA pair differs in power.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v2_6.12.6.q: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
o: There exist context-free languages such that all the context-free grammars generating them are ambiguous
An unambiguous context-free grammar always has a unique parse tree for each string of the language generated by it
Both deterministic and non-deterministic pushdown automata always accept the same set of languages
A finite set of string from some alphabet is always a regular language
go_v2_6.12.6.e:
**(A) True.** Some CFLs are *inherently ambiguous*, meaning every grammar for them is ambiguous.
- A standard example is $\{a^i b^j c^k \mid i = j \text{ or } j = k\}$.
- Strings $a^n b^n c^n$ belong to both halves of the "or", and every grammar must give them two parse trees.

**(B) True.** This is the definition of an unambiguous grammar: each string in its language has exactly one parse tree, or equivalently one leftmost derivation.

**(C) False.** Non-deterministic PDAs are strictly more powerful than deterministic ones; the DCFLs are a proper subset of the CFLs.
- For example, the even-length palindromes $\{ww^R\}$ are accepted by an NPDA, which guesses the middle of the input.
- No DPDA accepts this language.

**(D) True.** A finite set $\{x_1, \ldots, x_k\}$ is described by the regular expression $x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k$, so it is regular.

**Answer: (C)**

go_v2_6.14.2.q: A language $L$ satisfies the Pumping Lemma for regular languages, and also the Pumping Lemma for context-free languages. Which of the following statements about $L$ is TRUE?
o: $L$ is necessarily a context-free language, but not necessarily a regular language.
go_v2_6.14.2.e:
**Key idea.** Both pumping lemmas give necessary conditions, not sufficient ones. Every regular language satisfies them, but some languages that are not even context-free satisfy them too.

**Counterexample:** $L = \{a^ib^jc^kd^l \mid i = 0 \text{ or } j = k = l\}$.

- **$L$ satisfies the regular pumping lemma with $p = 1$.** Pump the first symbol of any non-empty $s \in L$. If $s$ starts with $a$, then $j = k = l$, and changing the number of leading $a$'s keeps the string in $L$: either some $a$'s remain and $j = k = l$ still holds, or no $a$'s remain and $i = 0$. If $s$ starts with $b$, $c$ or $d$, then $s \in b^*c^*d^*$, and pumping its first symbol keeps it in $b^*c^*d^*$ with $i = 0$.
- **The regular pumping lemma implies the context-free one.** Given a split $s = xyz$, use $u = x$, $v = y$, $w = x' = \epsilon$, $y' = z$.
- **$L$ is not context-free.** $L \cap ab^*c^*d^* = \{ab^nc^nd^n \mid n \ge 0\}$ is not context-free, and context-free languages are closed under intersection with regular languages.

So such an $L$ need not be regular, or even context-free, which rules out (A) and (B). Option (C) is false because every regular language also satisfies both lemmas.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v2_6.15.1.q:
Let $Q = (\{q_1, q_2\}, \{a, b\}, \{a, b, \perp\}, \delta, \perp, \phi)$ be a pushdown automaton accepting by empty stack for the language which is the set of all nonempty even palindromes over the set $\{a, b\}$. Below is an incomplete specification of the transitions $\delta$. Complete the specification. The top of the stack is assumed to be at the right end of the string representing stack contents.

1. $\delta(q_1, a, \perp) = \{(q_1, \perp a)\}$
2. $\delta(q_1, b, \perp) = \{(q_1, \perp b)\}$
3. $\delta(q_1, a, a) = \{(q_1, aa)\}$
4. $\delta(q_1, b, a) = \{(q_1, ab)\}$
5. $\delta(q_1, a, b) = \{(q_1, ba)\}$
6. $\delta(q_1, b, b) = \{(q_1, bb)\}$
7. $\delta(q_1, a, a) = \{(\ldots, \ldots)\}$
8. $\delta(q_1, b, b) = \{(\ldots, \ldots)\}$
9. $\delta(q_2, a, a) = \{(q_2, \epsilon)\}$
10. $\delta(q_2, b, b) = \{(q_2, \epsilon)\}$
11. $\delta(q_2, \epsilon, \perp) = \{(q_2, \epsilon)\}$
go_v2_6.15.1.e:
**Key idea:** a nonempty even palindrome has the form $ww^R$ with $w \neq \epsilon$. The PDA pushes $w$ in state $q_1$, nondeterministically guesses where the middle is, and then pops while matching $w^R$ in state $q_2$.

- Rules 1–6 push every symbol read in $q_1$. Rules 3 and 6 are the only ones that read the symbol currently on top of the stack.
- The first symbol of $w^R$ equals the last symbol of $w$, which is on top of the stack. So at the middle, reading $a$ with $a$ on top (or $b$ with $b$ on top) must also offer "pop and switch to matching mode":
$$7.\ \ \delta(q_1,a,a) = \{(q_2,\epsilon)\} \qquad 8.\ \ \delta(q_1,b,b) = \{(q_2,\epsilon)\}$$
  Together with rules 3 and 6 this gives $\delta(q_1,a,a)=\{(q_1,aa),(q_2,\epsilon)\}$ and $\delta(q_1,b,b)=\{(q_1,bb),(q_2,\epsilon)\}$. This is the nondeterministic guess of the middle.
- In $q_2$, rules 9 and 10 pop one matching symbol per input symbol. Rule 11 removes $\perp$, leaving the stack empty, which means acceptance.
- The empty string is not accepted. Reaching $q_2$ requires at least one push in $q_1$ and one matching pop, so only nonempty strings $ww^R$ reach an empty stack.

**Trace for $abba$** (top of stack at the right):

| Step | Input read | State | Stack |
|---|---|---|---|
| start | – | $q_1$ | $\perp$ |
| rule 1 | $a$ | $q_1$ | $\perp a$ |
| rule 4 | $b$ | $q_1$ | $\perp ab$ |
| rule 8 | $b$ | $q_2$ | $\perp a$ |
| rule 9 | $a$ | $q_2$ | $\perp$ |
| rule 11 | – | $q_2$ | empty: accept |

**Answer: 7. $\delta(q_1,a,a)=\{(q_2,\epsilon)\}$; 8. $\delta(q_1,b,b)=\{(q_2,\epsilon)\}$**

go_v2_6.15.3.q:
Let $M = (\{q_0, q_1\}, \{0, 1\}, \{z_0, X\}, \delta, q_0, z_0, \phi)$ be a Pushdown automation where $\delta$ is given by
$$\begin{aligned}
&\delta(q_0, 1, z_0) = \{(q_0, Xz_0)\}\\
&\delta(q_0, \epsilon, z_0) = \{(q_0, \epsilon)\}\\
&\delta(q_0, 1, X) = \{(q_0, XX)\}\\
&\delta(q_1, 1, X) = \{(q_1, \epsilon)\}\\
&\delta(q_0, 0, X) = \{(q_1, X)\}\\
&\delta(q_0, 0, z_0) = \{(q_0, z_0)\}
\end{aligned}$$

a. What is the language accepted by this PDA by empty stack?

b. Describe informally the working of the PDA
go_v2_6.15.3.e:
**Key observation:** the only move that can empty the stack is $\delta(q_0,\epsilon,z_0)=\{(q_0,\epsilon)\}$. It needs state $q_0$ with $z_0$ on top, and no move ever pops $z_0$ in $q_1$.

**(a)**
- While $M$ is in $q_0$ with only $z_0$ on the stack, each $0$ leaves everything unchanged, by $\delta(q_0,0,z_0)$. At any point $M$ may pop $z_0$ by the $\epsilon$-move. After that the stack is empty and no further move is possible, so this accepts exactly when the whole input has been read. This accepts $0^n$ for every $n \ge 0$, including $\epsilon$.
- Once a $1$ is read in $q_0$, an $X$ is pushed on top of $z_0$. From then on $z_0$ is covered:
  - In $q_0$ with $X$ on top, further $1$'s push more $X$'s, and a $0$ moves $M$ to $q_1$.
  - In $q_1$, each $1$ pops one $X$. But $q_1$ has no move on input $0$, no move with $z_0$ on top (in particular no $\delta(q_1,\epsilon,z_0)$), and no way back to $q_0$.
  - So $z_0$ is never removed, and no input containing a $1$ can empty the stack.

Hence
$$N(M) = \{0^n \mid n \ge 0\} = 0^*.$$
Since the set of final states is $\phi$, nothing is accepted by final state.

Examples:
- $00$: $(q_0,00,z_0)\vdash(q_0,0,z_0)\vdash(q_0,\epsilon,z_0)\vdash(q_0,\epsilon,\epsilon)$, accepted.
- $101$: $(q_0,101,z_0)\vdash(q_0,01,Xz_0)\vdash(q_1,1,Xz_0)\vdash(q_1,\epsilon,z_0)$, stuck with $z_0$ on the stack, so rejected.

**(b) Informal working.**
1. In $q_0$, $M$ skips a leading block of $0$'s, keeping $z_0$.
2. It then counts a block of $1$'s by pushing one $X$ per $1$.
3. It treats a single $0$ as a separator and switches to $q_1$.
4. In $q_1$ it cancels one $X$ for each following $1$.

So it appears designed to check strings like $0^m1^k01^k$ (equal blocks of 1's around a 0). However, it lacks a move such as $\delta(q_1,\epsilon,z_0)=\{(q_1,\epsilon)\}$ to remove the bottom marker. Every such computation therefore dies with $z_0$ still on the stack. The only computations that empty the stack are those that read $0$'s in $q_0$ and then pop $z_0$ by the $\epsilon$-move.

**Answer: (a) $N(M) = 0^* = \{0^n \mid n \ge 0\}$**

go_v2_6.15.5.q:
A push down automation (pda) is given in the following extended notation of finite state diagram:

**Figure:** states $q_0$ (initial) and $q_1$; edges:
- $q_0 \to q_0$ (self-loop): $1, s/1.s$
- $q_0 \to q_1$: $2, s/s$
- $q_1 \to q_1$ (self-loop): $1, 1.s/s$

The nodes denote the states while the edges denote the moves of the pda. The edge labels are of the form $d, s/s'$ where $d$ is the input symbol read and $s, s'$ are the stack contents before and after the move. For example the edge labeled $1, s/1.s$ denotes the move from state $q_0$ to $q_0$ in which the input symbol $1$ is read and pushed to the stack.

A. Introduce two edges with appropriate labels in the above diagram so that the resulting pda accepts the language $\{x2x^R \mid x \in \{0,1\}^*, x^R \text{ denotes reverse of x}\}$, by empty stack.

B. Describe a non-deterministic pda with three states in the above notation that accept the language $\{0^n1^m \mid n \leq m \leq 2n\}$ by empty stack
go_v2_6.15.5.e:
**A.** The given machine already does three things:
- in $q_0$ it pushes every $1$;
- on the centre marker $2$ it moves to $q_1$ without touching the stack;
- in $q_1$ it pops a $1$ for every $1$ read.

The two missing edges do the same for the symbol $0$:
- $q_0 \to q_0$: $0, s/0.s$ (read 0 and push it);
- $q_1 \to q_1$: $0, 0.s/s$ (read 0 with 0 on top and pop it).

After reading $x$ in $q_0$, the stack read from top to bottom is $x^R$. After the $2$, state $q_1$ can empty the stack only by reading exactly $x^R$. A mismatch or a second $2$ leaves the machine stuck, and a nonempty input with no $2$ leaves symbols on the stack. So the machine accepts $\{x2x^R\}$ by empty stack.

**B.** *Idea:* push one $0$ for every input $0$. Then cancel each stacked $0$ with either one $1$ or two $1$'s, chosen nondeterministically. The number of 1's then lies between $n$ and $2n$.

States: $q_0$ (reading 0's), $q_1$ (matching 1's), $q_2$ (the first 1 of a pair has been read and its pop is pending).

| Edge | Label | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $q_0 \to q_0$ | $0, s/0.s$ | push a 0 for each input 0 |
| $q_0 \to q_1$ | $1, 0.s/s$ | one 1 cancels one 0 |
| $q_0 \to q_2$ | $1, 0.s/0.s$ | first 1 of a pair, no pop yet |
| $q_1 \to q_1$ | $1, 0.s/s$ | one 1 cancels one 0 |
| $q_1 \to q_2$ | $1, 0.s/0.s$ | first 1 of a pair |
| $q_2 \to q_1$ | $1, 0.s/s$ | second 1 of the pair pops the 0 |

Acceptance is by empty stack after the whole input has been read.

**Why it works.**
- Every one of the $n$ stacked 0's must be popped. Each pop consumes either one 1 or a pair of 1's (through $q_2$, where the stack is never empty).
- Hence $m = n + (\text{number of pairs})$ with $0 \le \text{pairs} \le n$, which gives $n \le m \le 2n$. Every such $m$ is reachable by choosing $m-n$ pairs.
- A 0 after a 1 has no move, so it is rejected. For $n = 0$, only $\epsilon$ is accepted.

Example $00111$: push, push; $q_0 \to q_1$ pops; $q_1 \to q_2$ no pop; $q_2 \to q_1$ pops. The stack is empty, so the string is accepted ($n=2$, $m=3$).

**Answer: A: add $0, s/0.s$ on $q_0$ and $0, 0.s/s$ on $q_1$. B: the three-state NPDA in the table above.**

go_v2_6.15.6.q: Give a deterministic PDA for the language $L = \{a^ncb^{2n} \mid n \geq 1\}$ over the alphabet $\Sigma = \{a, b, c\}$. Specify the acceptance state.
go_v2_6.15.6.e:
**Idea:** push two $X$'s for every $a$, so that $n$ $a$'s leave $2n$ $X$'s. After the $c$, pop one $X$ for every $b$. When the bottom marker $Z_0$ reappears, move to the accepting state.

$M = (\{q_0, q_1, q_f\}, \{a,b,c\}, \{X, Z_0\}, \delta, q_0, Z_0, \{q_f\})$, with the top of the stack written leftmost:

| Move | Purpose |
|---|---|
| $\delta(q_0, a, Z_0) = \{(q_0, XXZ_0)\}$ | first $a$: push two X's |
| $\delta(q_0, a, X) = \{(q_0, XXX)\}$ | each further $a$: two more X's |
| $\delta(q_0, c, X) = \{(q_1, X)\}$ | read $c$ (only after at least one $a$) |
| $\delta(q_1, b, X) = \{(q_1, \epsilon)\}$ | each $b$ pops one X |
| $\delta(q_1, \epsilon, Z_0) = \{(q_f, Z_0)\}$ | all X's matched: go to $q_f$ |

All other moves are undefined, which means reject. **Acceptance state: $q_f$** (acceptance by final state).

**Deterministic.** Each (state, input, top) triple has at most one move. The only $\epsilon$-move, $\delta(q_1,\epsilon,Z_0)$, has no competing input move on $Z_0$ in $q_1$.

**Correctness.**
- $\delta(q_0,c,Z_0)$ is undefined, so $n \ge 1$ is enforced.
- With fewer than $2n$ $b$'s, the machine ends in $q_1$ with an $X$ on top, which is not accepting.
- With more than $2n$ $b$'s, the extra $b$ finds $Z_0$ in $q_1$ (or the machine is already in $q_f$), and no move exists.
- Any $a$ after $c$, or a second $c$, also has no move.

**Trace for $acbb$:**
$(q_0, acbb, Z_0) \vdash (q_0, cbb, XXZ_0) \vdash (q_1, bb, XXZ_0) \vdash (q_1, b, XZ_0) \vdash (q_1, \epsilon, Z_0) \vdash (q_f, \epsilon, Z_0)$, accepted.

(An equivalent design pushes one $X$ per $a$ and pops one $X$ for every two $b$'s, using an extra state to count $b$'s in pairs.)

**Answer: The DPDA above; it accepts by final state $q_f$.**

go_v2_6.15.13.q:
Let $P$ be a non-deterministic push-down automaton (NPDA) with exactly one state, $q$, and exactly one symbol, $Z$, in its stack alphabet. State $q$ is both the starting as well as the accepting state of the PDA. The stack is initialized with one $Z$ before the start of the operation of the PDA. Let the input alphabet of the PDA be $\Sigma$. Let $L(P)$ be the language accepted by the PDA by reading a string and reaching its accepting state. Let $N(P)$ be the language accepted by the PDA by reading a string and emptying its stack.

Which of the following statements is TRUE?
o: $L(P)$ is necessarily $\Sigma^*$ but $N(P)$ is not necessarily $\Sigma^*$.
$N(P)$ is necessarily $\Sigma^*$ but $L(P)$ is not necessarily $\Sigma^*$.
go_v2_6.15.13.e:
**Key idea:** the PDA is always in its accepting state, but a string counts as accepted only if the PDA can actually **read the whole string**. That depends on the transition function, which is not given. The PDA may have no move for some input symbol, or it may empty its stack early and halt.

Counterexamples:
- **No transitions at all.** Nothing beyond $\epsilon$ can be read, so $L(P) = \{\epsilon\}$. $Z$ is never popped, so $N(P) = \emptyset$. Neither is $\Sigma^*$.
- **$\Sigma = \{a,b\}$ with only $\delta(q,a,Z) = \{(q,Z)\}$.** Here $L(P) = a^*$, not $\Sigma^*$.
- **Only $\delta(q,a,Z) = \{(q,\epsilon)\}$.** Here $N(P) = \{a\}$, not $\Sigma^*$.

Both languages *can* equal $\Sigma^*$. For example, $\delta(q,\sigma,Z)=\{(q,Z)\}$ for every $\sigma$ gives $L(P)=\Sigma^*$, and adding $\delta(q,\epsilon,Z)=\{(q,\epsilon)\}$ also gives $N(P)=\Sigma^*$. But nothing in the description forces this.

Hence neither $L(P)$ nor $N(P)$ is necessarily $\Sigma^*$.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v2_6.15.14.q: Which of the following languages is accepted by a non-deterministic pushdown automaton (PDA) but NOT by a deterministic PDA?
o: $\{a^l b^m c^n \mid l \ne m \text{ or } m \ne n\}$
go_v2_6.15.14.e:
**Key idea:** We need a language that is context-free but **not** deterministic context-free (DCFL). Use the fact that DCFLs are closed under complement and under intersection with regular languages.

**(B) is context-free.** $L_B = L_1 \cup L_2$ with $L_1 = \{a^l b^m c^n \mid l \ne m\}$ and $L_2 = \{a^l b^m c^n \mid m \ne n\}$. A PDA for $L_1$ pushes the $a$'s, pops one per $b$, and accepts if the counts differ (a $b$ arrives with no $a$ left, or $a$'s remain when the $b$'s end), reading the $c$'s freely; $L_2$ is handled the same way with $b$ against $c$. A non-deterministic PDA guesses at the start which condition to check, so $L_B$ is a CFL.

**(B) is not a DCFL.** If $L_B$ were deterministic, then $\overline{L_B}$ would be a DCFL, and so would
$$\overline{L_B} \cap a^*b^*c^* = \{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \ge 0\}.$$
But that language is not even context-free (pumping lemma). This is a contradiction.

**Other options:**
- (A) $\{a^nb^nc^n\}$ is not context-free, so no PDA of either kind accepts it.
- (C) $\{a^nb^n\}$ is a DCFL: push on $a$, pop on $b$, accept on reaching the bottom marker. Every move is deterministic.
- (D) $\{a^mb^n\} = a^*b^*$ is regular, so a DPDA (even a DFA) accepts it.

**Answer: (B)**
